Moltrech tree frog (Rhacophorus moltrechti) is an arboreal amphibian endemic to Taiwan, where it occupies montane and lowland forests. Newly emerged hatchlings from gelatinous egg masses are notably diminutive, with a wet weight at birth of merely 0.036 grams [Wwb = 0.036 grams]. This initial body mass is constrained by the yolk reserves available within each individual egg and sets the energetic baseline for the subsequent larval phase. The aquatic tadpoles, which are exogenously feeding and actively growing, undergo a complete morphological transformation culminating in metamorphosis. By the time tail resorption and limb development are complete, the newly terrestrial froglets achieve a wet weight at metamorphosis of 0.8 grams . This nearly twenty-two-fold increase in mass from the hatchling stage to the end of the larval-juvenile transition reflects the high productivity of the aquatic foraging environment. The precise timing of these developmental milestones is temperature-dependent; however, under standard laboratory conditions maintained throughout the year, embryonic development proceeds rapidly, with the eggs hatching after approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] when incubated at 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

Following the transition to land, the recently metamorphosed juveniles, often termed froglets, enter a prolonged period of somatic growth during which they must acquire sufficient resources to reach reproductive maturity. The post-metamorphic interval required for the onset of gonadal maturation and the attainment of puberty is considerable. Data from captive-reared cohorts suggest that, when maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time since metamorphosis at puberty is approximately 91.5 days [tp = approximately 91.5 days]. This period of roughly three months allows the froglets to increase substantially in both skeletal size and body mass before allocating energy to gametogenesis. The relatively extended duration of this juvenile phase, compared to some lowland congeners, may reflect the cooler thermal regime of montane habitats, which suppresses metabolic rates and slows the accumulation of body reserves. By the time individuals reach sexual maturity, they have attained a body mass that supports the energetic demands of amplexus, egg production, and foam nest construction.

Reproductively active females of Rhacophorus moltrechti exhibit a strategy of repeated breeding across a single season, depositing multiple clutches to maximize annual fecundity. Field observations and captive breeding records indicate that each female typically produces between 100 and 300 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 100 and 300 eggs per clutch], a broad range that likely reflects variation in female body size and nutritional condition. Furthermore, individuals are capable of depositing three clutches per year [F_R_i = three clutches per year] during favorable weather, allowing for a substantial total annual reproductive output. The construction of foam nests, which are affixed to vegetation overhanging still water, provides protection against desiccation and predation during the embryonated egg stage. This high fecundity is characteristic of many rhacophorid frogs and is thought to compensate for significant egg and larval mortality in the ephemeral aquatic habitats they exploit. The trade-off between clutch size and egg size is a central determinant of offspring quality, and the observed range in clutch size suggests a degree of phenotypic plasticity.

As individuals continue to grow beyond the onset of reproduction, they eventually approach their maximum skeletal dimensions and asymptotic body mass. The ultimate snout-vent length for adult Moltrech tree frogs reaches approximately 5.6 centimeters [Li = approximately 5.6 centimeters], a size that is typical for medium-sized members of the genus Rhacophorus. Concomitant with this skeletal attainment, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is around 6.4 grams [Wwi = around 6.4 grams], providing a robust estimate of the body size at which growth effectively ceases and all available energy is directed toward reproductive effort and daily metabolic costs. This species thus exhibits a life history in which a substantial fraction of the lifespan is spent at a stable adult body size, with relatively little further increase in mass after the attainment of maximum length. The relationship between length and mass in this species is congruent with allometric patterns observed in the family Rhacophoridae, where larger females generally achieve higher clutch volumes.

Longevity data for Rhacophorus moltrechti in natural settings remain limited, but captive maintenance under controlled environmental conditions offers useful insights. When housed at a stable temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] with adequate nutrition and humidity, individuals have been documented to survive for as long as 22 years [am = 22 years]. This remarkably extended lifespan is among the longest recorded for any rhacophorid frog and suggests a slow pace of life that may be linked to the lower and more predictable metabolic demands of a cool, stable thermal environment. Such longevity allows for multiple reproductive seasons, offsetting the lower per-season fecundity that would be predicted by a "live slow, die old" strategy. The interplay between a long reproductive window and moderate annual fecundity ultimately determines the lifetime fitness of this species. Understanding how temperature influences these demographic parameters is critical for predicting population resilience in the face of climate change, particularly for range-restricted montane endemics.
